name: Kesavan
role: Weigher at the port steelyards, the large and small dacing

flaw.text: Kesavan will not trust a weight he has not taken himself. His inspections are sound but slow, and a ship he is weighing may hold its berth past the hour it should have left.

bio: A Kling from the Coromandel coast who came to Melaka as a cloth broker's clerk and stayed to work the steelyards. He knows which goods go on the large dacing and which on the small, and he can feel a false weight in the beam before the pointer settles. He has never once hurried.

assign: Berths, Shahbandar? I weigh cargo. Very well, I will keep the order you give me, exactly.
I will follow the list. If the list is wrong, I will follow it anyway.
good: Every ship went in the order you set. I wrote down the hour of each.
The berths turned over as planned. No one argued with the list.
mixed: I kept your order, but a rice boat came in after you wrote it, and I did not dare change it. She is still at anchor.
The order held, but it was slow. I checked every captain's name twice.
bad: I held a berth for a ship that never came, as the list said. Two others waited all day.
I am not the man for the water, Shahbandar. The anchorage is full and the berths are half idle.

assign: I will put every lot on the beam. Spices on the large dacing, tin and silk on the small. It will take as long as it takes.
Give me the declaration. The steelyard will tell us what is true.
good: Every lot weighed true to its declaration. You may clear her with a quiet mind.
I found the fault. The pepper was reckoned in small bahar, and pepper goes on the large. The difference is written here for the temenggung's bench.
mixed: The weights are right. The quality I cannot swear to. My beam does not taste pepper.
I weighed two lots in three. The ship must sail, so the last one went ashore on the captain's word.
bad: I weighed every lot and found nothing, and the ship lost her sailing time while I did it. She left angry, half unsold.
The weights were honest. What was wrong was inside the bales, and I did not open them.

assign: I will buy by weight and only by weight. No one cheats me on the beam.
I will see the goods weighed before a single calain changes hands.
good: Bought and weighed in. The treasury has exactly what it paid for, to the kati.
A fair price on honest weights. The seller tried a light beam once. Only once.
mixed: The weight is right, but the price was high. The seller knew I would not leave until it was weighed.
We have the goods, but I spent the morning weighing and the best lots went to others.
bad: I argued over every kati until the merchant sold to the Chinese buyers instead. We have nothing.
Correct weight, poor grade. I should have looked as well as weighed.

notes: [FACT] Heavy bulk goods were weighed on a beam steelyard, the dacing (Portuguese dachem), and Melaka used a large and a small bahar of 200 kati each for different goods: pepper and other spices on the large, tin and China silk on the small (Nunes, Livro dos Pesos, 1554, ed. Felner 1868, p. 39; docs/research/ships-weights-currency.md §2.1).
[FACT] Pires records a separate weighing due on goods weighed in or out, handled by the king's secretaries and receivers (Pires, p. 274; port-official.md §5.1).
[FACT] The Klings had more of the Melaka trade than any other nation (Pires, p. 272).
[INFERENCE] No named weigher is recorded; a Kling clerk working the steelyards is a plausible type, not a documented person.
[GAMEPLAY] Kesavan is a fictional character. Flaw weighs_everything: his delegated inspections take longer, which can cost a ship its berth time or sailing.
